content: 1. Delirium and confusional states refer to conditions of impaired consciousness, often associated with acute or chronic cerebral or organic diseases. These states are clinically characterized by disorientation, slowed mental processes, apathy, lack of initiative, fatigue, and poor attention. In mild cases, rational responses may be elicited, but severe cases can render individuals unable to maintain contact with their environment. 2. Alzheimer’s disease is a primary degenerative cerebral disorder of unknown cause in most cases. It is marked by specific neuropathological and neurochemical changes. The disease typically has an insidious onset and progresses slowly but steadily over several years. 3. Anticholinergic side effects occur when medications block the effects of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. These effects include dry mouth, urinary frequency or retention, palpitations, and sinus tachycardia. 4. Ataxia is a failure of muscular coordination caused by dysfunction in parts of the nervous system that control movement and balance. It can affect the fingers, hands, arms, legs, body, speech, and eye movements. 5. Autonomy refers to an individual’s perceived ability to control, cope with, and make personal decisions about their daily life according to their own rules and preferences. 6. Behavioral activation is a psychological treatment aimed at improving mood by re-engaging individuals in task-oriented and previously enjoyable activities, even during periods of low mood. It can be used as a standalone treatment or as part of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). 7. Bereavement is the process of experiencing loss, grief, and recovery, typically associated with the death of a loved one. 8. A cerebrovascular accident, or stroke, is a sudden disturbance of cerebral function caused by vascular disease, such as thrombosis, hemorrhage, or embolism. 9. Cognitive processes involve mental activities such as reasoning, remembering, judgment, problem-solving, and planning. 10. Comorbidity refers to the simultaneous presence of two or more diseases or disorders in an individual. 11. Confusion or confusional states are conditions of impaired consciousness associated with acute or chronic cerebral or organic diseases. Symptoms include disorientation, slowed mental processes, apathy, fatigue, and poor attention. 12. Contingency management therapy is a structured method of rewarding desired behaviors, such as attending treatment or avoiding harmful substance use. Over time, external rewards are reduced as natural rewards become established. 13. Convulsions, or convulsive movements, are disturbances of cortical function caused by sudden, abnormal, excessive, and disorganized discharges of brain cells. Clinical manifestations include abnormal motor, sensory, and psychic phenomena. 14. Detoxification is the process of safely withdrawing an individual from the effects of a psychoactive substance, minimizing withdrawal symptoms. 15. Disability refers to any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in a manner considered normal for a human being, resulting from an impairment. 16. Disinhibited behavior is characterized by a lack of restraint, disregard for social conventions, impulsivity, and poor risk assessment. It can affect motor, emotional, cognitive, and perceptual aspects of functioning. 17. Disorganized or disordered thinking involves disturbances in associative thought processes, often evident in speech where the individual shifts abruptly between unrelated topics without awareness of the disconnection. 18. Distractibility is the difficulty in concentrating and focusing on tasks, with attention easily diverted by external stimuli. 19. Dystonia involves sustained muscle contractions or involuntary movements that can lead to fixed abnormal postures. 20. Eclampsia is a condition affecting pregnant women, characterized by seizures or convulsions, often associated with pregnancy-induced hypertension, severe headache, blurred vision, proteinuria, and edema. 21. Elevated mood is a positive emotional state marked by increased energy and self-esteem, which may be disproportionate to the individual’s circumstances. 22. Extrapyramidal side effects or symptoms (EPS) are abnormalities in muscle movement, often caused by antipsychotic medications. These include muscle tremors, stiffness, spasms, and akathisia. 23. Family therapy involves multiple planned counseling sessions over months, delivered to individual families or groups, often including the person with mental illness. It provides support, education, and problem-solving or crisis management. 24. Focal deficits are observable neurological signs that indicate the location of a specific lesion in the nervous system. 25. Hallucinations are false perceptions of reality, such as seeing, hearing, feeling, smelling, or tasting things that are not real. 26. Hepatic encephalopathy is an abnormal mental state, including drowsiness, confusion, or coma, caused by liver dysfunction. 27. Hyperarousal is an intense and prolonged autonomic discharge, often seen in post-traumatic stress disorders (PTSD), characterized by heightened alertness and watchfulness. 28. Hypersensitivity reactions are adverse effects of pharmaceutical formulations resembling allergies. These are dose-independent, unpredictable, and can manifest in various clinical phenotypes. 29. Idiosyncratic reactions are individual, unpredictable, and non-dose-dependent responses to substances, such as drowsiness, euphoria, or flushing. 30. Informed consent is the process by which a healthcare worker provides appropriate information to a person, enabling them to make a voluntary decision to accept or refuse treatment. 31. Interpersonal therapy (IPT) is a psychological treatment focusing on the link between depressive symptoms and interpersonal problems, such as grief, disputes, life changes, and social isolation. 32. Irritability or irritable mood is a state characterized by being easily annoyed and provoked to anger, often disproportionate to the circumstances. 33. Motivational enhancement therapy is a structured therapy lasting up to four sessions, aimed at helping individuals with substance use disorders by discussing their substance use and encouraging self-determined goals. 34. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare but life-threatening condition caused by antipsychotic medication, characterized by fever, delirium, muscular rigidity, and high blood pressure. 35. Occupational therapy helps individuals improve independence in daily living activities through rehabilitation, exercises, and assistive devices. It also promotes growth, self-fulfillment, and self-esteem. 36. Oppositional behavior is marked by defiance, disobedience, and provocative or spiteful actions, often accompanied by persistent anger, irritability, and severe temper outbursts. 37. Parent skills training involves teaching parents emotional communication, positive parent-child interaction skills, and reinforcement methods to improve children’s behavior and functioning. 38. Polytherapy refers to the use of more than one medication simultaneously for the same condition. 39. Privacy is the state of being free from unauthorized intrusion, such as maintaining confidential health records. 40. Problem-solving counseling is a psychological treatment involving systematic problem identification and solving techniques over multiple sessions. 41. Pseudodementia is a disorder resembling dementia but not caused by organic brain disease and potentially reversible with treatment. It may manifest as depressive symptoms in older adults. 42. Psychoeducation involves teaching individuals with mental, neurological, and substance use disorders, as well as their caregivers, about the nature of the illness, its causes, progression, consequences, prognosis, and treatment options. 43. QT prolongation is a medication-induced side effect characterized by a prolonged QT interval on an ECG, which can lead to ventricular arrhythmias and increased risk of sudden cardiac death. 44. Racing thoughts refer to rapid thought patterns with tangential movement from one idea to the next, often associated with mania or other mental illnesses. 45. Relapse is the return to substance use or the recurrence of symptoms of mental, neurological, or substance use disorders after a period of recovery. 46. Relaxation training involves techniques such as breathing exercises to elicit a relaxation response. 47. Respiratory depression is an inadequately slow breathing rate, leading to insufficient oxygen intake, often caused by medications like benzodiazepines. 48. Respite care provides temporary care in a healthcare facility for individuals normally cared for at home. 49. Rigidity is resistance to passive limb movement throughout its range, often a symptom of parkinsonism. 50. Seizures are episodes of brain malfunction due to cortical disturbances, resulting in sudden, abnormal, excessive, and disorganized brain cell discharges. Clinical manifestations include abnormal motor, sensory, and psychic phenomena. 51. Self-harm refers to intentional self-inflicted poisoning or injury, which may or may not have fatal intent or outcome. 52. Serotonin syndrome is caused by an excess of serotonin in the central nervous system, often due to medications like SSRIs. Symptoms include muscle rigidity, myoclonus, agitation, confusion, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia, and dysautonomic symptoms, with risks of shock, seizures, coma, rhabdomyolysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). 53. Slurred speech refers to indistinct pronunciation of words. 54. Social networks are constructs in analytical sociology that examine the characteristics of social linkages among people to understand their behavior. 55. Social withdrawal is the inability to engage in age-appropriate activities or interactions with peers or family members. 56. Status epilepticus is defined as five or more minutes of continuous seizure activity or recurrent seizures without recovery between episodes. It can be convulsive or non-convulsive. 57. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a life-threatening skin condition characterized by painful skin peeling, ulcers, blisters, and crusting of mucocutaneous tissues, often caused by severe reactions to medications, especially antiseizure drugs. 58. Stigma refers to a distinguishing mark that leads to social exclusion and discrimination, often creating an additional burden for individuals with mental illness. 59. Suicidal thoughts or ideation involve thoughts or plans about ending one’s life, ranging from passive wishes to elaborate plans. 60. Tardive dyskinesia is a form of dystonia involving twisting and sustained muscle spasms, often affecting the head, neck, and occasionally the back. It may persist even after stopping antipsychotic medication. 61. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a life-threatening condition involving severe skin peeling, usually caused by a reaction to medication or infection. It is more severe than Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
